Answer: When determining the depth of design drawings, it is essential to balance three key factors: design quality, engineering budget, and the level of detail in the drawings. If the drawings are overly detailed, they will consume excessive time and may lead to budget overruns; if they are too simplistic, they may fail to meet design quality requirements.

Commercial and industrial projects differ significantly in terms of budget. Generally, industrial projects have much higher design budgets than commercial ones. This is because industrial projects are typically larger in scale, allowing for relatively ample design budgets. For example, just the technical specifications, purchase orders, and related requirements for a single switchgear cabinet can require approximately 40 work hours. Take generator projects as another example: the design cost for a few hundred-kilowatt generator in a civil project might be around 20,000–30,000 RMB, whereas industrial projects require more specialized efforts for detailed design, with final costs potentially reaching hundreds of thousands of RMB—almost equivalent to the price of the generator itself.

There are also notable differences between North America and China in engineering design. First, design fees are higher in North America, typically ranging from 5% to 10%, while in China, they are only 1%–3%. Second, the design cycle for North American projects is longer, often lasting one to two years; in contrast, Chinese projects have shorter design cycles, with even large-scale projects completing preliminary designs in just 1–2 months.

These differences result in the following outcomes: North American designs are more thorough and comprehensive but progress more slowly, while Asian regions excel in speed. In North America, most issues must be resolved during the design phase; otherwise, immature designs will lead to frequent changes during construction, making cost control more difficult. For projects of the same scale, the time and cost required for implementation in North America are at least five times higher than in China, which is closely tied to its stringent process control systems.

In North America, construction specification books (book spec) have specialized templates. The United States has its own template, and Canada has its own, but the two templates are fundamentally similar.  

The American template is developed by the American Institute of Architects (AIA) and is called MasterSpec, while the Canadian version is known as the National Master Specification (NMS). These templates are already quite comprehensive, as will be shown later. They account for various possible scenarios, which is why they are referred to as “Master.” When using them, you only need to select the relevant content based on project requirements or delete unnecessary sections, eliminating the need to write from scratch and saving significant time.

The numbering system for specifications transitioned from five digits to six digits, a change that occurred roughly over a decade ago. Each specification has a numerical code and a corresponding title that describes its specific content. The entire system is divided into 44 Divisions, such as Division 0001, which will be demonstrated in detail later.

These templates require payment to access. In Canada, the template for just the mechanical and electrical sections alone costs around CAD 2,000. The entire template system is updated periodically, but unlike codes that are revised every three or five years, updates may occur every three to five years or sometimes annually. Answer: In North America, the engineering license systems in the United States and Canada differ. Individual U.S. states have their own licensing systems, similar to driver’s licenses; Canadian provinces also implement comparable systems. In Canada, if an engineer already holds a license in one province, applying for a license in another province typically does not require retaking exams—only submitting an application and paying the fee is needed. For example, applicants with a good record in Ontario can usually obtain a license in British Columbia by completing the formalities.

The requirements for obtaining a license in both the U.S. and Canada include at least one year of domestic work experience, as well as a bachelor’s degree or higher recognized by the engineering association. Additionally, applicants must have four years of professional work experience, with at least one year completed within Canada. As a result, engineering qualifications obtained in other countries may not be directly transferable in North America.

During the application process, aside from meeting the education and work experience requirements, applicants must also provide recommendation letters from two professional engineers.
